title: Broncos and Bo Nix are targeting subtle area of improvement in QB's third year Bo Nix has made "noticeable strides" in the way he's shown patience with initial reads, resulting in big-play opportunities Nick Kosmider

full_text:
Sean Payton intimated there are opportunities for Bo Nix, right, to stick longer at times with the early reads in his progressions. Ron Chenoy / Imagn Images
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Bo Nix escaped and scrambled to his right during a training camp practice last week as defensive backs blanketed his targets and the pass rush closed in around him. The Denver Broncos quarterback turned upfield and sprinted toward the safety who was dropping down to cut off his progress. Then, Nix planted his right foot firmly in the ground and sharply cut inside to continue his run.
Coach Sean Payton has described the traits displayed by Nix in that sequence as his “superpower.”
The evasiveness has helped the Broncos take sacks over the past two seasons at easily the lowest rate in the NFL (3.8 percent of dropbacks). The quarterback’s explosiveness and getaway speed in the open field have helped the Broncos win games, too. Like when he sprinted into the end zone on a combined quarterback crack run in the fourth quarter of a thrilling comeback against the New York Giants. Or when he darted into the open field to push Denver into field-goal range during another final-drive win, this one in Houston. Only Buffalo’s Josh Allen has more quarterback runs of 20 or more yards than Nix (nine) over the past two seasons.
Yet, for all the positives Nix’s feet can produce, the Broncos are targeting a subtle change with their franchise quarterback in his third year that could reduce the frequency with which he relies on them.
“He does a very good job of avoiding the sack, the minus play,” Payton said last week when asked for an area he’d like to see Nix improve in 2026. “Then, because of that, he’s very good with his progression. I mean, clean with it. He’s not someone who’s … slow to process; it’s the other way. So there are sometimes where he’s through one (progression) so fast. … But I’d rather deal with that than the slow processor who’s getting sacked.”
The Broncos have had, by far, the NFL’s best sack differential over the past two seasons (plus-84; 53 points better than the second-ranked L.A. Rams). It is a critical part of their winning formula and a far cry from the minus-10 figure during Payton’s first season in Denver in 2023 with Russell Wilson at quarterback. That’s why Payton made clear the Broncos aren’t trying to keep Nix from accessing a strength that has ample benefits for Denver’s offensive attack. But the coach intimated there are opportunities for Nix to stick longer at times with the early reads in his progression.
“He’s a real good foot athlete,” Payton said. “You don’t feel someone who’s cumbersome at all. I think it’s one of his gifts. Within the framework of each pass play, the (defining) of a three (step drop), three-no-hitch, one big five (step-drop) and a hitch, some of those specifics that put him exactly in time with the depth of the route, I think is something I’m sure he’s working on.”
When Davis Webb was named the Broncos offensive coordinator in February, he quickly went to work on a project with the team’s passing-game staff that served as a deep audit of Nix’s first two seasons as the team’s quarterback. The big-picture goal was to identify how to best build upon Nix’s strengths in ways that benefit the efficiency of the offense as a whole. One aspect of that work, Webb said last week, was making sure routes were being designed to complement the way in which Nix scans the field.
“He’s definitely progressing in that area,” Webb said. “There were some long areas in the offseason with the pass-game staff of really trying to evaluate and watch the last two years of him playing and, ‘How does the first read marry up with our second read depth-wise and play-call wise, (given) where we are at a point in the game?’ I think we’ve done a good job managing that. … I think it’s noticeable the strides he’s taken in hanging on one (read), getting to two and three, and then getting to his legs.”
Webb said he sees a progression with Nix that closely mirrors where Allen was as he entered his third NFL season. The Buffalo quarterback in 2020 — Webb was one of the team’s backups that season — posted a 107.2 passer rating that still stands as the best in his career. He made the Pro Bowl for the first time as his completion percentage jumped from 58.8 as a second-year starter in 2019 to 69.2. Allen benefited that season from the arrival of standout receiver Stefon Diggs, and Webb said in the spring he views new Broncos receiver Jaylen Waddle as a similarly impactful addition.
“I think he’s right on par with the other guys I’ve been around going into Year 3,” Webb said. “I’m really satisfied where he’s at, both getting in and out of plays, getting to the huddle, getting in and out of the huddle fast, checking plays when it’s appropriate, not overthinking, getting completions underneath and using his feet. I think the injury last year, it was important for him to kind of move around a little bit early here, and I think he’s done a really good job. I’m really satisfied with where he is.”
The Broncos’ veteran defense has provided ample opportunities to test the tweaks the Broncos are making offensively. Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph has shown Nix “every defensive structure imaginable” during the camp’s first three weeks, the quarterback said Monday. Joseph on Saturday credited the way Nix has found answers to the new ways in which he’s being challenged, noting that the quarterback’s deep-ball accuracy has been “off the charts” in camp.
“It’s safeties from everywhere, blitzes from everywhere, fronts from everywhere,” Nix said of the defense. “That just helps you as a quarterback get your eyes up and then slow the game down once you get into a game setting. For me, it’s been irreplaceable to go against VJ, and not only his defense, but I can ask him questions and figure out the ‘why’ behind some things.”
One sign Nix is working on sticking with first reads a little bit more when circumstances allow: He is actually throwing in the direction of All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II. The quarterback during his first two training camps would quickly zoom past his first read if that receiver was being defended by Surtain, a decision commonly made during the season by opposing quarterbacks. In this camp, though, Nix hasn’t been shy about going after Surtain. Success has been predictably limited, but it sheds light on the comfort level Nix has to experiment with things as he prepares for his third season.
“My first two years, if he was over there, I pretty much worked the other side of the field,” Nix said. “But I don’t think that does him (due) diligence. (Let’s) get him better at the same time. I don’t mind throwing it his way and getting an incompletion on the stat sheet just to help him out. And then, every once in a while when you do complete one on him, it’s good for the morale of the offense and shows us we’re also really good and can attack the best player in football on the defense.”
The Broncos will play at least some starters Friday in their preseason opener at Atlanta, but Payton declined to say whether Nix would see the field in a game for the first time since suffering a broken ankle during the playoff win against the Bills. The quarterback, after two offseason procedures on that right ankle, has had a full workload running the first-team offense in camp, and Payton said last week that Nix’s “movement that we’re seeing right now is back to where it was.” That was evident as Nix sprinted into the open field while running the same quarterback sweep play that resulted in that aforementioned touchdown against the Giants.
The Broncos finished Monday’s practice with a tweak to their normal schedule. After end-of-workout wind sprints, the team separated into lines for another stretching session, mirroring the one they conduct to begin practices. full_text:
Joshua Dobbs spent time with the Patriots last season and made a stop with the Lions in 2022. He's the front-runner to be Jared Goff's backup. Brian Fluharty / Imagn Images
ALLEN PARK, Mich. — Dan Campbell broke the news Sunday, and a day later, Teddy Bridgewater took to Instagram to confirm it.
He’s retiring from the NFL . For good.
“This time, it’s official,” Bridgewater wrote Monday on Instagram. “It’s so crazy 10 years ago around this time, I suffered one of the most gruesome knee injuries the game itself, its players and some doctors had ever seen. Everything football-related since 2016 had been fueled by the “experts” predicting that I would never play football again. We really showed them by playing 10 more seasons! However, this wheel of mine can no longer deal with something so simple as standing around on the turf field. This thing just doesn’t recover the same way it did years ago so I’d rather officially hang it up. It’s finally run its course and when the body speaks to me, I have to listen so that I can be in one piece and available for my children as they grow up. The game of football was beyond great to me and owes me nothing at all. I really did things my way.”
Based on Bridgewater’s comments, the knee injury he suffered in 2016 with the Minnesota Vikings was a factor in this decision — in addition to his desire to be healthy for his family. Bridgewater is preparing for the birth of his daughter in a couple of weeks, and if the pain was enough that he didn’t feel right while simply standing on turf, it makes sense to retire. The fact he made it this far is a testament to his resilience.
What does it mean for the Detroit Lions’ backup QB job? It’s worth discussing.
There’s a story Campbell often tells when asked to describe his thoughts on Bridgewater. It was 2019, and Drew Brees suffered a torn UCL — a thumb injury to his throwing hand. He was set to miss significant time, and the New Orleans Saints’ playoff hopes were in Bridgewater’s hands.
Campbell will never forget it.
“Drew got injured, we had just gone out to the Rams, got beat out there, and Drew got his thumb, and we lost him for five weeks, and Teddy stepped in,” Campbell recalled. “We won five in a row, man. And that was Teddy. And then just his time being with us meant a lot, and it meant a lot to our guys. So, he’s going to be missed.”
During his time with the Lions, Bridgewater was credited with helping Jameson Williams develop into a professional and offering guidance and mentorship to a young locker room. During the 2024 playoffs, Bridgewater was forced into action when Goff briefly left to be evaluated for a concussion and oversaw a touchdown drive. He’s been a calming presence in more ways than one.
The Lions lost key veteran voices this offseason: Alex Anzalone, Amik Robertson, DJ Reader, Taylor Decker, Kalif Raymond — leaders in their position groups. And though the Lions believe their replacements can be trusted to fill the void, it didn’t hurt to add one of the most respected players in the league, Bridgewater. It’s a role that would’ve fit him well, but given what we now know, his decision is understandable.
Bridgewater is moving on, and the Lions are, too.
The majority of Goff’s backups have been either veterans who’ve started games and been around the block or smart quarterbacks on a coaching trajectory.
Former Lions QB David Blough fits the latter. Coaches raved about his intelligence and ideas when he was here. He’s now the offensive coordinator of the Washington Commanders, and the Lions even showed interest in Blough for their own OC opening this offseason before the Commanders promoted him. It’s why Detroit kept him around despite his physical limitations.
Then there’s the experienced journeymen we’ve seen in past training camps. Nate Sudfeld, Kyle Allen and Bridgewater have spent at least a full season backing up Goff and have been credited for being sounding boards for QB1. Lions quarterbacks coach Mark Brunell has talked about the role of a backup when it comes to supporting the starter.
“It’s very important for a starter to have a resource on the sideline — a backup guy who just wants Jared to be the best he can be,” Brunell said in 2023. “It makes all the difference in the world.”
That’s what Bridgewater was, and it’s what the Lions wanted to add when the news was announced. The Lions have typically leaned toward this type of QB. They’ve tried the developmental route in the past when they used a third-round pick on Hendon Hooker, but he was cut before the start of his third NFL season. Finding an experienced QB to pick up the offense two weeks into training camp is less than ideal, but the Lions might’ve found a perfect man for the job.
The Lions moved quickly to replace Bridgewater, signing veteran Joshua Dobbs on Sunday. Dobbs spent part of the 2022 season with the Lions, but the Tennessee Titans signed him off Detroit’s practice just weeks later. Before that, Dobbs spent part of the 2022 season with current Lions OC Drew Petzing, who was Dobbs’ QBs coach with the Cleveland Browns that season. When Petzing left Cleveland to become the OC of the Arizona Cardinals in 2023, Dobbs joined him.
Among the free-agent QBs available, Dobbs made the most sense as a smart veteran with experience and familiarity with Petzing’s terminology. Dobbs, who graduated from Tennessee with a 4.0 GPA in aerospace engineering, is viewed as a quick study and high-character individual. He owns a career passer rating of 78.3 and has 15 career starts. He fits the mold of what the Lions look for in a backup, and his ability to help starters is one of the reasons teams keep calling.
“We signed Josh Dobbs,” Campbell said Monday. “We had a short period with him (in 2022). Man, it’s been a while now. But man, we really liked him. And then he got poached, and so, that’s kind of where it went, but it’s good to get him back. Just saw him this morning. He’ll be out there running around. We probably won’t give him any reps, but just get him up to speed off on the side. And so, it’s good to have him”
“Josh and I met in high school at the Elite 11, 15 years ago or so,” Goff said. “I’ve known Josh for a long time, competed against him. He was here for, what was it, 10 days or something? He was great to have in the room then, and I’m excited to have him back.”
And then there’s Luke Altmyer, a rookie UDFA who’s been with the team since April. Altmyer has been running the second- and third-team offense in camp, albeit with ups and downs. He’s mobile, and when he has time to let it rip, he’s shown solid accuracy. However, Altmyer threw two interceptions as the No. 2 QB during Monday’s practice. It comes with the territory.
“We like Luke,” Campbell said. “Luke is growing, Luke is getting better, he just needs reps. I mean, he needs a million reps. But the reps that he has gotten to this point, he has improved. And so we like him, but we are going to add somebody.”
The Lions will give Altmyer a long look in the preseason — especially early, as Dobbs gets up to speed on the offense. Based on how the Lions have typically approached this backup job, Dobbs is likely to make the roster as Detroit’s No. 2 (barring a collapse), and Altmyer could be more of a practice-squad option to stash until he becomes more.
We’ll see whether the preseason changes that narrative. The Lions kick things off at 7 p.m. Thursday versus the Bengals in Cincinnati.

title: Packers coach Matt LaFleur found new perspective after a rocky 2025 season. Can he keep it? The regular season will bring new challenges, but for now, LaFleur is finding value in understanding the things he can't control. Jourdan Rodrigue 1

full_text:
Matt LaFleur is entering his eighth season as head coach of Green Bay. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; John Fisher / Getty
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Matt LaFleur is trying to let go of his anger about things he can’t control. In his office on a Sunday morning in early August, the printer did not count as one of them.
LaFleur, the Green Bay Packers head coach now entering his eighth season in the role, wanted to print his practice scripts and call sheets for that day, but the machine was glitching. Nobody was around to help troubleshoot the problem. So LaFleur started yelling at it.
“I was livid. I couldn’t get anybody to help,” he said, laughing.
That, LaFleur admitted, was ultimately a waste of energy. He made fun of himself — “I didn’t respond the right way this morning,” he cracked — but in truth, he’s been thinking a lot about this topic over the last few months.
“I don’t think I get as pissed off as I used to,” he said. “… I’m just like, ‘All right, am I in control of this? Or not?’ … I think a little bit more like that (or at least try to) with a lot of things. … That has helped me, when I know I can’t control it.”
LaFleur has sometimes given the impression that he always has to be right, that he always has an answer or a rebuttal. His quickness can translate to excellent problem-solving on the field (just look at what he did with backup quarterback Malik Willis, helping the third-round pick-turned-backup become a QB1 again with the Miami Dolphins). But like most NFL coaches, LaFleur will admit that his acuity can also be a gateway to anger or frustration when things don’t go how he plans.
I expected a typical conversational path with LaFleur when we sat down that day, one that had very little to do with him and instead was a careful deflection back to the smart scheming and planning for the season ahead. But he was different. LaFleur began talking about what he can and cannot let go of. His shoulders slumped briefly, and he looked away.
This was grief, sudden and relentless.
Cristina Ulbrich, wife of Atlanta Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich — the couple, longtime friends of LaFleur and his wife, Bre — had died just a few days earlier from cancer. She was 48 .
LaFleur had planned to attend her memorial service, flying privately so as to quickly make it out of one long, work-intensive training camp day and return before another started. As the plane he commissioned prepared to take off, the crew found a mechanical issue, and he got stuck. He ultimately had to return to the Packers’ facilities while Bre traveled separately and made it in time to support Ulbrich and his family. LaFleur said he felt terrible about missing the service. How jarring, to pivot right back to football as a friend was laid to rest.
“All the sudden, I’m back in meetings,” he said, wincing. “I’m like, ‘ It’s out of my control .’”
Cristina — her illness, her passing, how Ulbrich must feel — keeps coming into LaFleur’s mind. He pictures the hurt in Ulbrich’s face. LaFleur, his younger brother Mike (the Arizona Cardinals’ first-year head coach), Ulbrich and Tennessee Titans head coach Robert Saleh, plus their wives and kids, have been friends for years, bonded by various coaching jobs and connecting friendships, and by the unrelenting grind of football. LaFleur, 46, has known loss before. But this was different. Cristina was one of them . She was part of the fabric of their peer group, intertwined with the peaks and valleys of their football lives as much as their family lives.
“It’s different … when it’s somebody your age,” LaFleur said quietly. “She was a rock star. I think about it every day. I worry about ‘Brich.”
LaFleur gestured around his large office. “It puts all of this stuff a little bit more in perspective,” he said, “… you can’t take it for granted, that’s for sure.”
The barely controlled chaos of an NFL head coaching job during a day of training camp was on full display in LaFleur’s office. One wall is actually a giant dry-erase board, covered in hand-drawn plays. Another features a massive screen that is a backdrop for the large, curved double monitors on LaFleur’s desk, surrounded by scribbled-on practice script cards and play call sheets.
The computer screens all had a different tab open, from emails to film clips to roster notes and more. LaFleur suddenly remembered he had forgotten to eat lunch between meetings, practice and interviews, so his assistant brought him a bowl of raw vegetables.
LaFleur keeps his phone in his office, and throughout that day he checked for updates from Saleh as the two discussed how to support Ulbrich in the coming days. Another group chat that includes longtime friend and former boss Kyle Shanahan provided updates on Shanahan’s health as he recovers from his July car crash .
Bre even stopped by with their oldest son after practice to say hello. The office may be all football, all the time, but there’s a lot of life happening there too.
Despite LaFleur’s moments of grief and worry, he also seemed … calm.
At least, he was calmer than expected for a man who had just experienced a season like the one the Packers had in 2025. Many, many things went sideways for LaFleur and his team despite beginning the year with such optimism and expectations.
New team president Ed Policy and longtime general manager Brian Gutekunst made bold moves in the 2025 draft by selecting Matthew Golden at No. 23, the first receiver taken by Green Bay in the opening round in over two decades. They were bold again in their trade for elite pass rusher Micah Parsons right before the season began, sending multiple first-round picks plus defensive tackle Kenny Clark to the Dallas Cowboys. These would be the “new Packers,” they seemed to express — built solidly out of NFL history and tradition but now willing to take bigger swings. With both LaFleur and Gutekunst coming due for contract extensions, it felt like the organization had dared the perennially winning head coach and GM to go bolder, too.
But then, both Parsons and tight end Tucker Kraft, who was quickly ascending and bringing the Green Bay offense along with him, got hurt. Other key role players did too. A 5-1-1 start became a 9-7-1 finish (and let’s not even talk about that tie ).
Quarterback Jordan Love also got banged up and had to sit out a game at the end of the season before the team’s underwhelming playoff exit in the wild-card round to the rival Chicago Bears. LaFleur, who has the third-best winning percentage among active NFL head coaches, at times drew the ire of Packers fans for his situational decision-making and for what looked like confusion in a crowded and inconsistent receivers room. In the offseason, defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley left for the head coaching job in Miami, and respected special teams coordinator Rich Bisaccia resigned.
It was “a weird year,” LaFleur admitted, with a lot of change — some of which he could control, some of which he couldn’t. As he nears a decade as a head coach, LaFleur thinks he’s learning to accept that.
“I think my perspective has changed a little bit, just on life in general,” he said. “The older you get, all you can ask of anybody is just do the best you can. … If you’re doing the best you can and it doesn’t work out, I can still look myself in the mirror and know I did everything I could. I feel like that about everyone in the building.”
In the spring, the Packers parted ways with receivers Romeo Doubs in free agency and Dontayvion Wicks via a trade with the Philadelphia Eagles. The remaining receivers and Love have felt more clarity within their group, plus Kraft figures to be back by Week 1 if not sooner. Parsons could return in October .
LaFleur also hired former Cardinals head coach Jonathan Gannon as his new defensive coordinator. He and Gannon had never worked together, but from their interview, LaFleur said, he “knew (Gannon) was a good person and knew he knew ball.” They hit it off quickly once Gannon arrived in Green Bay,…

full_text:
Quarterbacks Kyler Murray (1) and J.J. McCarthy (9) have been competing to be the Vikings' starter. Neither has been particularly impressive so far. David Berding / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — The Minnesota Vikings entered training camp with two primary objectives.
They wanted to figure out which quarterback gave them the best chance to win in 2026. And they wanted to make that decision with enough time to appropriately prepare the starter for Week 1 against the Green Bay Packers.
These two goals always seemed somewhat at odds . The present situation is not alleviating any of those concerns.
Before this past weekend, all signs pointed to the Vikings naming Kyler Murray the starter in the near future. Since then, neither Murray nor J.J. McCarthy has performed at a clip that makes the impending decision clear to any objective observer. Yet Minnesota is fast approaching the first preseason game and joint practices with the Baltimore Ravens, two essential points on the calendar in terms of how coach Kevin O’Connell prepares his team for the season.
“As I tell our guys every night and every chance I talk to them, we’ve got time, but not that much time,” O’Connell said Sunday evening.
So there’s some urgency regarding the need to make a decision. But it also highlights the current dilemma.
Keeping the competition going would validate O’Connell’s insistence that the team is holding a fair fight with no preconceived plan. Doing so, however, could come at the expense of making sure the first-team offense is as ready as possible in a system predicated on precision.
On the other hand, pronouncing Murray the winner after several poor performances — including, most notably, Sunday night — would suggest that he was ticketed to be the starter all along.
Either path would hold major ramifications for the quarterbacks and the team. For example, the fewer reps Murray receives in this new, complex offense, the more difficult it will be for him to get comfortable if he becomes the starter. Conversely, the fewer opportunities the Vikings give McCarthy, the more it will call into question the team’s choice to split reps between the two from the beginning.
There is an even more sobering possibility: that the attention on reps avoids harsher truths about the talent level of both quarterbacks.
“The elevator effect of that position is real,” O’Connell said. “Just like it can be a subtractor as well.”
The Vikings are still in the early stages of training camp, but the inconsistency of the passing game mirrors many of the concerning issues from last fall.
Defensive pressure has forced anxiety in the pocket. Coverage variance has muddied space over the middle. Offensive highlights emerge here and there, but the overriding daily takeaway tends to revolve around hope for an overhauled run game .
On Sunday evening, O’Connell pinned some of the poor results on the offense working through new schematic layers. He even suggested some practice struggles have been the byproduct of receivers taking the incorrect angles or directions on routes.
“It might be a small detail, but it’s important, and it affects the visual outcome of the play,” O’Connell said. “Where maybe us as coaches love those plays because you can really highlight it, get a correction and move forward.”
These miscommunications also surfaced in the first practices in shells. Murray, for example, attempted several downfield throws, where the receiver broke off a route rather than running vertically. In other instances, Murray lofted passes toward receivers whose depth didn’t match the target of the throw.
Murray counterbalanced some of these issues with a willingness to target superstar receiver Justin Jefferson and push the ball deep. On Aug. 1, the veteran QB staked his first real claim for the job.
Stacking more solid practices would have provided some separation, but he hasn’t done it.
McCarthy’s introductory phase featured mostly checkdowns, which came after multiple hitches. But his play improved this weekend. He completed one of his most impressive camp throws Sunday night in front of fans at TCO Stadium, an anticipatory corner route to receiver Myles Price near the left sideline.
This throw and others like it set the table for McCarthy to snatch some of the momentum. Instead, he misfired in the back half of the practice, often holding the ball and fidgeting in the pocket under duress.
The offense’s struggles should be taken with a grain of salt because the Vikings defense has been one of the league’s best units in recent years. Third-year edge rusher Dallas Turner is ripping around the edge with speed. Defensive tackle Jalen Redmond continues to cause problems on the interior. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores has not shied away from sending blitzers from the second level. Second-team offensive snaps against the first-team defense demand an even higher level of operation.
It’s also worth noting that former Vikings quarterback Sam Darnold, who won a Super Bowl with the Seahawks last season, struggled until the second day of joint practices during training camp in 2024.
But even this hits on the overarching point. McCarthy’s torn meniscus allowed Darnold to take 100 percent of the first-team snaps from Aug. 14 through the end of training camp. Deploying a similar timeline would require the Vikings to finalize their quarterback in four days — a declaration that would require extensive explanation.
“You start looking at reps, and it’s pretty darn close to 50-50,” O’Connell said. “And I think it’s really shown us a wide variety of things we can coach off of, such as improvement, comfort in the scheme, comfort in the experience in the scheme. How we project that moving forward is going to be based on whatever decision we make.”
Inspiring a shared level of conviction with the eventual decision is a significant part of this competition.
Last year, the Vikings entered the season with many inside the building questioning the path that had been taken. That cloud of frustration hovered over everything.
This time around, the Vikings committed to a different path. O’Connell welcomed the training camp discomfort, believing that pitting Murray against McCarthy would bring out the best in them and galvanize the entire team.
As long as that initial vision comes to fruition, the door to more second-guessing will remain shut.

full_text:
After years of struggles, the Giants are vibing off John Harbaugh's commanding presence. Ryan Hunt / Getty Images
WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — When John Harbaugh got the call from Baltimore Ravens owner Steve Bisciotti while driving home from the team’s training facility on Jan. 6 — and learned that his key card was being revoked — he experienced the disorienting shock that often accompanies such moments.
Fired after 18 seasons as the Ravens’ coach, an event set in motion two nights earlier when a rookie kicker shanked a field goal that would have clinched the franchise’s seventh AFC North title and 13th playoff appearance of his tenure, Harbaugh was overcome with angst and uncertainty about his future.
It was a sobering sensation — and it lasted about as long as the first quarter of an NFL game.
Within 45 minutes, seven teams — more than one of which hadn’t yet fired its current coach — had reached out to Harbaugh’s agent, Bryan Harlan, to inquire about his availability. That list would grow to at least nine teams in the coming days. By the time Harbaugh signed a five-year, $100 million contract to coach the New York Giants on Jan. 17, he carried himself with the breezy swagger of a man who’d been led to the edge of the cavernous fire pit, only to realize he had celestial wings.
Seven months later, Harbaugh’s unbothered aura has only gotten stronger. And everyone associated with the Giants, an organization mired in a decade-and-a-half-long recession, is vibing off the 63-year-old coach’s confident and commanding presence.
He fully expects to make the Giants better from the jump, and I’m convinced he’s correct.
“I feel really great about the situation, and I feel loose,” Harbaugh told me after a recent practice at the Greenbrier Resort’s Sports Performance Center, where the Giants spent the first two weeks of training camp. “You know, they tell the Marine snipers, ‘Stay loose, stay focused.’ You’ve got to be both. You can’t be focused and tight, and you can’t be loose and undisciplined.”
As Harbaugh quickly clarified, those snipers confront stakes far more serious than anything the sport of football can throw at a head coach.
“This is different,” he noted. “It should be easy to do it here.”
Reminding Giants players and coworkers that trying to win football games isn’t a “life or death” matter has been a frequent Harbaugh theme since he made the trip up the Eastern seaboard.
Sometimes, that messaging isn’t subtle. In June, I sat with Harbaugh on one of the buses transporting players, coaches and staff from the Giants’ training facility in East Rutherford, N.J., to Lower Manhattan for an unannounced trip to the 9/11 Memorial & Museum. As we rolled through midtown, we could hardly believe that a quarter century had passed since the horrific attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.
“This will be really heavy,” Harbaugh said, “especially for the guys who don’t remember it — or who weren’t born yet.”
It was also illuminating and inspirational, partly because of the coach who led the team’s trip to the site of the deadliest terrorist attack in U.S. history. When the players gathered in an auditorium to begin the visit, Harbaugh’s command of the room was pronounced. Put it this way: All eyes were on him as he spoke, and not a single cell phone surfaced as he stood onstage.
While plenty of outsiders have attempted to clown him over a snippet of the speech he gave at the start of OTAs this spring, which went viral after the Giants shared it on social media, Harbaugh’s message is resonating with the people who actually matter.
“He pulls the best out of everybody,” second-year edge rusher Abdul Carter told me earlier this month.
Carter and his teammates are all ears, which is understandable. Coming off a 4-13 season in 2025 and a 3-14 campaign in ’24, the Giants — with one playoff victory and two postseason appearances since the 2011 season, when they captured their fourth Lombardi Trophy — have basically become the New York Jets with less bluster .
As one Giants source who interacts daily with the men in uniform put it, “These players were starving for direction. Now they have it.” The source spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss team matters candidly.
Since two-time Super Bowl-winning coach Tom Coughlin stepped down after the 2015 season, the Giants have had a succession of head coaches (Ben McAdoo, Pat Shurmur, Joe Judge, Brian Daboll) who were neither successful nor — based on the accounts of their coworkers — particularly captivating.
Harbaugh, who has won a Super Bowl and an NFL-record eight road playoff games, has the chops to generate buy-in from his players. And the way he speaks to them, as someone who knows exactly what he wants but isn’t consumed with flexing his own power, has resonated from the start.
“A lot of it comes down to accountability and vulnerability,” said Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, one of two former NFL head coaches (along with quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan) on Harbaugh’s staff. “Harbs demands accountability from everyone, including himself. He’s also very vulnerable in a positive way, which everyone appreciates more than you can imagine. He’s vulnerable with extreme confidence in who he is and how he leads.”
Already, Harbaugh has had to navigate some internal tension, including star defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence’s contract-related trade request (he was eventually dealt to the Cincinnati Bengals for the 10th pick in the 2026 NFL Draft) and Carter’s public criticism of teammate Jaxson Dart after the second-year quarterback introduced President Donald Trump at a rally.
Inside the building, none of it felt that jolting. Among his peers, Harbaugh, while projecting authority, has always stood out for his willingness to tolerate self-expression and big personalities amid the pursuit of a common goal.
As I reported in 2012, a Ravens team meeting that fall became so charged with player complaints, coming “very close to getting out of control,” that some witnesses were stunned. Harbaugh managed to hear out his critics, get control of the situation and convince everyone to move forward as a team.
Three months later, the Ravens won the Super Bowl.
I’m not saying these Giants will trigger a sequel to the Knicks’ ticker-tape parade come February, but I would be shocked if they’re not appreciably more competitive in 2026 — and on the road to bigger and better things.
There is cause for anticipatory excitement. New York’s defensive front, with a trio of talented edge rushers in Carter, Brian Burns and Kayvon Thibodeaux — and a fourth, No. 5 pick Arvell Reese, playing inside linebacker — has the potential to swallow up opponents. Dart, coming off a promising rookie season, will attempt to level up behind a strong offensive line and with a new target (tight end Isaiah Likely, poached from the Ravens via free agency) who should serve as a security blanket.
Dart and his teammates should also find plenty of comfort in looking to the sidelines and seeing a coach who ranks in the top 15 in regular-season victories (180) and top 10 in postseason triumphs (13). When your leader is that accomplished — and carries himself like a man who believes his plan will work — it’s hard not to put your head down and try as hard as you can to bring it to life.
Think Phil Jackson coming back to the Los Angeles Lakers in 2005, or the Houston Astros hiring Dusty Baker in 2020, or Sean Payton taking over the Denver Broncos three seasons ago. When a true pro enters the building and lays out his vision, it tends to be eye-opening.
Before too long, I expect we’ll all be able to see the difference.

full_text:
Terry McLaurin battled injury last season for the first time in his career, but he's ready for a resurgence. Derik Hamilton / Associated Press
ASHBURN, Va. — At last, normalcy has returned for Terry McLaurin.
Mentally, physically and spiritually, the Washington Commanders’ Pro Bowl wide receiver feels better than ever, and the signs of healing and growth have begun manifesting themselves everywhere.
For example, take a moment in last Friday’s training camp practice.
The 30-year-old McLaurin — entering Year 8 in the NFL — explodes off the line while matched up with fellow veteran Rasul Douglas, and Douglas promptly matches McLaurin’s strides and forces him closer to the left sideline as they race toward the end zone. The coverage is great, the placement of quarterback Jayden Daniels’ pass to McLaurin’s back shoulder is better, and McLaurin’s response is most supreme.
At the last second, the 6-foot, 210-pound McLaurin plants his left foot, pirouettes like a ballerina, simultaneously shoots up his hands, plucks the ball from the air and contorts his lower body to get both tiptoes down just across the goal line before tumbling to the ground. In an instant, McLaurin bounces to his feet, flips the ball aside, points at Douglas, nods and smiles.
Stunned that McLaurin managed to get both feet down and complete the tough catch, Douglas could only slap his teammate five. But of course McLaurin — the NFL’s leader in contested catches since his rookie year in 2019, according to Pro Football Focus — made another play. It’s what he does. Or, what he did from 2019 to 2024, when he established himself as one of the most consistently productive and reliable receivers in the league.
Then came 2025 — a tumultuous year wherein McLaurin found himself at odds with the franchise that drafted him in the third round out of Ohio State and whose fans rank him among the most beloved players of the last decade. Then, after resolving a lengthy contract dispute, McLaurin battled injury for the first time in his career. The strife and misfortune rocked the receiver emotionally and led to a grueling journey only exacerbated by struggles that saw his Commanders go from 12-5 with an NFC Championship Game appearance in 2024 to 5-12 and in need of another reset this past winter.
“This last year was the hardest year of my life — from the contract and getting hurt, and you know, I’ve been going through some stuff off the field, just personally,” McLaurin revealed Friday. “It’s been extremely challenging.”
But now, fully healthy and nearly a year after he received his three-year, $97 million contract extension , McLaurin counts his blessings.
“I’ve seen myself grow as a man, grow spiritually, and grow as a teammate,” McLaurin said. “So I just feel like I’m in a great space. … I wouldn’t trade anything because it’s built me into the person I am right now, and I just feel like I’m playing with a type of freedom that I haven’t had. So I’m just looking forward to spilling that out for my team this year.”
Washington and its fans certainly welcome a return to form from “Scary Terry.” For the first six seasons of his career, McLaurin represented one of the few bright spots and sure bets for an organization mired in dysfunction and change.
Two owners, four head coaches, four offensive coordinators, four wide receivers coaches, an astounding 15 starting quarterbacks, and yet, McLaurin always delivered. He recorded five straight 1,000-yard seasons from 2020 to 2024, and during his second Pro Bowl season (2024), racked up a career-high 13 touchdown catches.
“He’s been able to be consistent because he’s a disciplined route runner, and it says a lot of quarterbacks trust him and a lot of coordinators trust him because they’re trying to get him the ball,” Commanders wide receivers coach Bobby Engram explains. “The mentality of being a relentless competitor and truly believing every ball in the air is his ball, and he’s going to get it, that’s what makes him different.”
McLaurin always understood his importance to Washington’s offense and organization, or so he thought. But last offseason represented his first true exposure to the business of football — the ugly side of the game. As the Commanders’ view of McLaurin’s worth differed drastically from that of McLaurin and his camp, the wide receiver grappled with how to maintain his mental health and self-belief. Described by anyone close to him as a team-first player, McLaurin struggled with how to conduct himself during negotiations. At one point, he requested a trade despite his strong desire to remain loyal to his teammates.
Eventually, the sides agreed to an extension. But three weeks into the season, McLaurin again found himself in uncharted territory as a quad strain caused him to miss seven games. (McLaurin sustained the injury in Week 3, missed four games, played in Week 8, aggravated the injury and missed the next three.)
Asked to describe the toll both experiences took on him, McLaurin said, “I’ve been somebody who’s kind of struggled with worry, struggled with anxiety, sometimes not feeling good enough. So when you go through contract stuff, when you go through injury, it can kind of make you feel insecure at times.”
A 14-year NFL veteran who played for the Chicago Bears, Seattle Seahawks and Kansas City Chiefs, Engram knew all too well the struggles his star pupil encountered.
“I understood the business side, having played, so we had to let that work itself out, but you never stop supporting the man, and who he is outside of the player. That’s very important to me,” Engram said. “We knew how much he wanted to be with us and be engaged. It was a difficult time. And for any of us that have been injured, we know when guys aren’t around the team, you feel a certain distance, and I didn’t want him to feel that in any way because he was still such a big part of what we were doing.”
In addition to Engram, McLaurin said he leaned heavily on his wife, Caitlin, teammates and other family members and friends. The devout Christian also said he dug deeply into the Book of Proverbs to gain wisdom on how to deal with anxiety, worry and his identity outside of football.
“My faith has really taught me that Jesus is enough, and that I’m great as I am,” McLaurin said. “I learned when you go through those hard things, (God) is building your character. He’s building your resilience, and he’s building something in you for this world. … I just tried to rest in him and genuinely be a great person for the young guys on this team.”
During his recovery, and because he couldn’t help his team in any other way, McLaurin assumed a more vocal leadership role in the receivers room, something that didn’t always come naturally for him.
McLaurin eventually did return to the field, playing the final six games of Washington’s lost season. His 1,000-yard streak came to an end at five seasons as he finished the year with just 38 receptions for 582 yards and three touchdowns in 10 games. However, Engram and the Commanders view the growth McLaurin achieved as far more valuable for the long term.
“I just see a guy who’s really comfortable being a natural leader now,” Engram said. “It’s been a growth process since I’ve been with Terry. So I’m really proud of how he’s been intentional about that. The work ethic is there, playmaking is still there, but him using his voice more in the locker room has been big.”
Said Daniels, “His presence, his voice, I mean, this is a guy that’s been doing it for countless years. … He’s just a true pro, true vet. You guys see him after practice, coaching up the younger guys, giving the game back, the knowledge — just bringing that energy. So last year was last year, but, you know, now we’re happy to step forward.”
Like McLaurin, Daniels battled injury off and on during the 2025 season. McLaurin said he believes the two grew closer as teammates, taking turns encouraging each other. Now healthy again, they hope to spearhead a newly designed offense led by…

title: Cardinals GM Monti Ossenfort Said 6 Big Things Today: Carson Beck, Josh Sweat & More
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals are nearly done with training camp.
The Cardinals wrapped up a jog-through today and are set for one last practice tomorrow before officially wrapping things up here at State Farm Stadium.
Arizona made general manager Monti Ossenfort available for reporters today — here's our biggest takeaways from what he said:
The Cardinals have all of Paris Johnson Jr., Michael Wilson and Garrett Williams eligible for massive contract extensions, though Arizona hasn't inked any of the aforementioned players just yet.
"I think the track record here the last three years is we've done extensions before the season, during the season, after the season. I think as with any negotiation/extension, those things take time, and there's a lot of conversations that go on," Ossenfort said.
"Sometimes the timelines are different, and when those match up, and when those discussions can come to agreement. I don't think there's any hard or fast rule, and I think really they come by a case-by-case basis."
Names such as Hjalte Froholdt and Dante Stills are also possible names to watch.
LaFleur, entering his first season as a head coach, has arrived prepared according to Ossenfort.
"He's got a plan, and it's good to see. Not only just the offensive side of things, which obviously he's putting a lot of focus in there, but really the big picture and the whole team," said Ossenfort.
"When you sit in that chair, a lots on your plate in terms of organization, not just the football product, but it's everything that we do. Meeting schedule, practice schedule, how we travel, everything that goes into it, and he's been he's been ready for it. He's had a plan, and it's been exciting to watch him put it in place here over the last few weeks."
Beck has been the talk of the town really since he arrived in the desert, though last week's preseason performance has plenty of buzz around the third-round pick.
So far, so good from Ossenfort's standpoint.
"I thought he got off to a good start. I think the most optimistic thing was just the clean operation," said Ossenfort.
"The way they got in and out of the huddle, the way that he handled the checks that came his way, he got the ball out of his hand, put it in the right spot. He was accurate, so [a] very positive start. A good start. It kind of builds off of what he's been doing since he got here in the spring and the early part of training camp. Obviously still got a long way to go, but thought that was a good next step in his development."
The current starter, Jacoby Brissett, is still catching up to the team's playbook after recently ending his holdout. Brissett saw a restructured deal pay him at least $15 million guaranteed for 2026.
Why did the Cardinals negotiate with a player who was already under contract through this season and clearly was not part of their plans moving forward?
"I think when we signed him, it was in a different role, and so we signed Jacoby to be a backup quarterback, and his role changed. His job changed, and the expectation changed, and so really that is what it came down to," said Ossenfort, who also added:
"With what Jacoby did last year, what he meant to the locker room — I think you guys saw just the the reaction of his teammates and how excited they were — we were excited to get the deal done with him and move forward."
Sweat's been mentioned in consistent trade buzz after the Cardinals fired Jonathan Gannon, though the team is adamant Sweat will not only be healthy for the regular season opener as he manages a knee issue — Ossenfort says the team flat-out is not interested in trading him.
"I'd say [trade] discussions that come by that, there's always a lot of talk that goes around that. We have no interest in trading Josh. We're excited to have him," he said. "Some of those discussions [we're] going to keep private. But excited to have Josh here, [he] had a great year last year. Excited for more good things out of him this year."
Love, since arriving to the desert, has been a showstopper in nearly every opportunity. He looks the part, has proved he can get open as a receiver and obviously has hit some home runs when toting the rock.
Ossenfort had a laundry list of things he liked about the No. 3 overall pick:
"Mature, professional, eager to learn, very coachable, versatile, able to do a lot of different things with him. I think coachability is a big thing. Jeremiyah was obviously a very talented player coming out [as] a high draft pick, but his improvement over the last couple weeks, just with his running style and his reads, and putting his foot in the ground and getting upfield, I think we've seen growth in that in a very short time once the pads came on," said Ossenfort.
"That's great to see out of a young player that wants to learn, wants to contribute, wants to find a role for the team, and he's been great in that respect. So excited to keep using him in multiple ways, and he's a guy that's going to help us put pressure on the defense."

title: Cardinals GM Slams Door Shut on Josh Sweat Trade Rumors
full_text:
GLENDALE — Josh Sweat has made headlines throughout the 2026 offseason, and as the team ramps up for their second preseason game, the Arizona Cardinals' top sack artist still has yet to practice.
Sweat, placed on the Physically Unable to Perform list at the beginning of camp, hasn't been spotted on the sidelines during Cardinals training camp practices as he is working through a knee injury according to head coach Mike LaFleur.
While he can't technically practice due to his placement on PUP, Sweat was also not a participant during mandatory minicamp while he wasn't present during offseason team activities, either.
Trade buzz has followed Sweat since the Cardinals fired head coach Jonathan Gannon, someone Sweat was close to. Today, when speaking with reporters, general manager Monti Ossenfort shut those talks down.
"Josh is making good progress. Josh is getting closer every day. I think Josh is going to be out there in due time to get ready for the season opener, and we're excited to get him out there and get him going," said Ossenfort.
"I'd say [trade] discussions that come by that, there's always a lot of talk that goes around that. We have no interest in trading Josh. We're excited to have him. Some of those discussions [we're] going to keep private. But excited to have Josh here, [he] had a great year last year. Excited for more good things out of him this year."
Sweat, who just turned 29, reportedly had multiple NFL teams calling the Cardinals about his availability this offseason. Yet with a thin Cardinals pass rush room, it didn't make sense for the organization to part ways with their only productive outside linebacker.
Sweat's managing a knee issue, which has mostly led to his absence throughout the bulk of the offseason and camp. The Cardinals are confident he'll be ready for the start of the regular season.
"He's in all the meetings. He's around. I know I've said it, so broken record there, but he looks really good in terms of [being] healthy, in shape, all those kind of things," LaFleur said earlier in camp.
"He's putting a lot of work in behind the scenes to make sure when he gets the green light and everyone feels good. Ultimately [we're] making sure Josh feels good both mentally and physically to go out there and perform the way [he can] because he takes a lot of pride in what his product looks like. That tape matters a lot to him as I've gotten to know him. So he's earned the right to communicate with us to say, 'hey, I feel good, I'm ready to go.'"
It will be interesting to monitor how things go for the Cardinals this season and if their trade deadline plans change at all.
It's clear there's a market for Sweat.

title: The Disrespect Toward Cardinals Star Budda Baker Has Gotten Out of Hand
full_text:
ARIZONA — Earlier this offseason, I had a nice exchange with Budda Baker on X where he essentially called me out for not believing he deserved to be listed on the NFL's Top 100 players list, where he finished at No. 75.
My shock in his placement was more so rooted in the fact that Arizona was 3-14 last season, not that Baker didn't actually deserve it. I figured Trey McBride would make the list, surely, just based on the fact that he wrapped up one of history's greatest seasons ever for a tight end. I was even surprised Josh Sweat made it at No. 78 .
I bring up the above to say... Pro Football Focus' safety rankings ahead of the 2026 season are absolutely wild.
Baker found himself at the very bottom of PFF's list at No. 32 with the following explanation:
"An eight-time Pro Bowler, Baker is a well-respected player — but one whose advanced statistics paint a more cloudy picture. Baker has sat below a 65.0 overall PFF grade in two of the past three seasons, and his coverage was especially liable last year," wrote Bradley Locker.
"Indeed, Baker’s 35.7 PFF coverage grade was the third-lowest among qualifiers, giving up a 119.6 passer rating when targeted. Also worrisome for Baker was a career-high 17% missed tackle rate. The 30-year-old is still a formidable run defender, but his coverage acumen may not project well for the close of his career."
Even the biggest haters of the Cardinals or Baker would agree that's far too low. Baker just turned 30 and still should still produce at high levels for the next few years.
Is he the best cover safety? Not quite, as Baker's game more successfully operates in blowing up run plays and closing down on ball-carriers quickly near the line of scrimmage. Still, his pure talent and freedom to roam in Nick Rallis' defense brings an unknown factor that offensive coordinators have to essentially guess on every week.
Baker, even on his worst day, doesn't belong at No. 32 in any safety rankings.
There's time for Baker to flip the script ahead of 2026, where Rallis says the star safety has looked the best he has.
"I think he looks the best he's ever looked since I've been with him, to be honest. And that's real. He'll tell you that," said Rallis.
"He's moving so good because he's just on a different level in terms of how he takes care of himself, how he trains. I think that he feels phenomenal right now, and he looks phenomenal. He's got the play style, he's got the ability that he's always had. But you can just see that the work he puts in, he's still that missile. It's pretty cool to see."

title: Cardinals Finally Make Larry Fitzgerald Decision Fans Have Waited For
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are finally retiring Larry Fitzgerald's number.
After his induction into the Pro Football Hall of Fame this past weekend, the Cardinals are set to retire Fitzgerald's coveted No. 11 on Oct. 25 against the Denver Broncos.
"No one who has ever worn a Cardinals uniform is more deserving of this honor," said Michael Bidwill in a statement to the team.
"The thing I remember most about his presence here is not just how he practiced on the practice field but the way he took his profession so seriously. He is a pro's pro. His presence, both setting the tone but also welcoming people and in the locker room being a little bit of a jokester and wanting to engage everyone around him. He contributed so much to this organization and so much to this community. He means so much to us all."
Fitzgerald's gold jacket resume needs no introduction. Numerous Pro Bowls and NFL records are under his belt thanks to 17 years of high level play — all coming with Arizona.
Fitzgerald's No. 11 becomes the sixth jersey retired by the team, followed by:
For decades, Cardinals fans have loved Fitzgerald. Even after retirement, he's still one of the most popular jerseys you'll see around the desert.
During his Hall of Fame speech, he showed that same love back.
"I just want to show a little love to my Cardinal fans here in attendance today. To the Cardinal fans back home in Arizona, you guys supported us on and off the field over the years. You showed up at home games and showed up at away games, through wins and losses," he said.
"It's been 22 years and counting Arizona, and I'll spend the rest of my life trying to replenish the well of goodwill I've been lucky enough to drink from."
It was only a matter of time before Fitzgerald entered the Hall of Fame, and had his number retired. Is a statue next?
Possibly, but one step at a time. If anybody deserves the honor of having a statue outside of State Farm Stadium next to Pat Tillman, it's Fitzgerald.

title: Winners, Losers From Cardinals' Red and White Practice: Carson Beck Fires No-Look TD Pass
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals wrapped up what's likely their final open practice of 2026 with the famous Red and White scrimmage on Sunday.
Thousands of fans filled the lower bowl of State Farm Stadium as the team returned from a successful stint in Canton for Hall of Fame weekend.
The Cardinals practiced for two hours and gave fans plenty to talk about. Ranked, in no order, are our biggest winners and losers from today:
Love, who didn't suit up in Canton, got back to work and quickly reminded Cardinals fans of just how dominant he could be. Whether he was cutting up-field on runs or showing his prowess in either route-running or catching, Love's ability to win in either the pass or ground game was fully on display with the first-team offense today.
Jacoby Brissett didn't have a particularly strong or weak outing today, so it's tough to place him in either a winner or loser category. What we can say, however, is he and Harrison weren't able to connect on much of anything. Harrison was targeted five or six times with no receptions in team drills. Harrison's been able to make loads of plays in camp, though he was quiet today.
After impressing the entire football world against Carolina, Beck quickly came back down to earth again during the opening stages of Sunday's practice with some ball placement issues that were eventually paired with an interception — though he was hit while throwing. Beck responded with a dime down the right sideline in a two-minute drill followed by a no-look pass for a touchdown.
Carson Beck with a dot deep down the right sideline. Followed by a NO-LOOK pass for six. pic.twitter.com/xg8SsXBymE
That, with some work mixed with the second team, made for an overall strong day in a Cardinals quarterback room that couldn't really separate themselves.
Nolen left practice today with an unknown injury. During team activities, he appeared to be shaking his right hand before later leaving and not returning. This is the second time Nolen's left due to an injury this training camp, and his prior injury history last season again has fans anxious.
Walter Nolen just left the field with something Trainer follows him out Second time he’s left a practice with an injury pic.twitter.com/sPXRK7ntK9
Here's to hoping it was just a knock and he'll be ready to rock and roll.
The Cardinals saw all of Elijah Jones, Kitan Crawford and Eku Leota get reps with the first team today. Arizona placed safety Joey Blount on injured reserve today while Kei'Trel Clark also wasn't dressed, paving the way for Jones and Crawford to have a bit more rotation with the defense. As for Leota, he's a name to watch as he continues to rise up the depth chart in preseason play.
Allgeier told reporters one of the top things he was working on was his pass-catching ability. With Love leering behind him in the rotation, that feels like a must. So today when Allgeier saw two passes hit his hands before dropping both — one being wide open and all alone — it wasn't exactly an encouraging sign.
Robinson continues to have a strong training camp outing, winning one-on-one matchups and consistently using his raw blend of speed and power to put himself in the backfield. He had two "sacks" today (since they're not actually taking the quarterback down) and just might be preparing for that coveted leap so many want him to take.
I thought today would be a nice day to wear a navy blue polo with khaki pants. Besides looking like a grad assistant for Penn State or Navy, I was wandering the sidelines while several S.A.F.E. security folks surrounded the field (per usual doing big football events) were wearing the exact same outfit as me. I must have been confused with them four or five times, even getting some jokes from workers themselves. At least I can look the part in a potential interview if needed.

title: The 1 Thing Cardinals Want From Carson Beck After His Stunning NFL Debut
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck impressed the entire country on Thursday night.
Beck, a third-round pick, isn't expected to start for the Cardinals with Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew currently in store, placing a heavy importance on preseason play for the rookie passer.
So far, so good, as Beck nailed his NFL debut in the Pro Football Hall of Fame Game to the tune of completing 15-of-19 passes for 188 yards and one touchdown in just over one half of play. The Cardinals were considerably impressed, according to insiders .
His performance was so good it spurred national conversations around the possibility of him starting sooner as opposed to later.
Now, the Cardinals are back home at State Farm Stadium for a short week of preparation before heading to Las Vegas on Thursday to battle the Raiders.
What's head coach Mike LaFleur looking for out of Beck?
"To continue to stack," LaFleur said.
"One day at a time. Like, let's see what we can do today. That's in the past. What do we learn from it? Because there was a lot of great learning experiences from that game in terms of stuff that us as an offense, us as a team, but each player could do a little bit better."
The Cardinals scored on their final three offensive drives of the half with Beck under center. His poise, command, ball placement and willingness to spread the ball through the three layers of defense stood out against Carolina.
However, LaFleur doesn't want to get too high or too low on Beck. He just wants consistency, and so far, that's exactly what the Cardinals have seen.
"Consistency is the truest level of performance. To go out there and do it every single day, whether it be a preseason game, a practice, all those kind of things [is important]. And so you take it for what it is in that moment," said LaFleur.
"You asked me about Carson. Carson operated the offense. We got in and out of the huddle. He wasn't rushed. Thought his eyes, his rhythm, his timing were for the most part in a good spot. And he did that for, I'd say a three and a half hour window for him. It was a two hour window, right? Because he didn't play most of that second half. Okay, learn from it, reset. Now let's get back to work, right? And that's what he's going to do, and I can say that because I know what he's made of. I liked what that was, but now we got to go do it again, not in the game but in practice."
It's unclear how much Beck will play in Vegas, though with the Cardinals leaning towards sitting their starters, the Miami/Georgia product is sure to see plenty of action again.

title: 3 Cardinals Trade Candidates Who Could Be Moved Now, Later or Down the Road
full_text:
ARIZONA — We're near the end of training camp, and approaching the halfway point of preseason for the Arizona Cardinals.
The Cardinals are set to conclude 2026's iteration of camp within the next few days while traveling to Las Vegas for preseason battle two of four for the team. After this week, Arizona will reset at their base in Tempe moving forward.
The roster and its respective depth chart are taking shape, as players are rising and falling in the coaching staff's favor.
As such, for various reasons, players might be receiving trade calls from other teams or Arizona may be looking to ship out a veteran.
Trades can be completed now, and for this regular season, the deadline is Tuesday, Nov. 10.
One candidate to be traded now (preseason), later (deadline) and down the road (after the regular season):
Why Cardinals Could Trade Trey Benson Now: Benson hasn't quite lived up to the billing for his tenure in Arizona thus far, and the Cardinals made that clear after signing Tyler Allgeier and drafting Jeremiyah Love this offseason. Benson is now battling with Bam Knight for RB4 duties — and if you ask us — he's on the outside looking in of the roster.
The Cardinals would be wise to field offers on Benson and recoup something rather than flat-out cutting him ahead of the regular season. The problem? He's still rehabbing from meniscus surgery last season and doesn't look promising to make an appearance during preseason play.
Why Cardinals Could Trade Gardner Minshew Later: You practically see it every year: a team looking to contend wants to beef up their quarterback room ahead of the postseason with a veteran passer. Minshew perfectly fits that bill both as both a low-cost/high-value backup and perfectly expendable quarterback.
Jacoby Brissett is set to be the immediate starter while Carson Beck might just be ready to step into action sooner as opposed to later. The Cardinals need to know what they have in Beck, making him a strong candidate to play this season — and Minshew an even stronger candidate to be traded.
Why Cardinals Could Trade Josh Sweat Down The Road: This wouldn't be until after the 2026 season, though if we're projecting trade candidates, this might be Arizona's strongest bet. Sweat reportedly requested a trade this past offseason and hasn't touched the field yet for the Cardinals. While his absence on PUP is strictly injury related, things have undoubtedly been weird around Sweat.
Where that could come into play is next year, where the Cardinals likely won't turn themselves into a playoff squad in 2026 and Sweat — already paid by the organization — may want to find a second wind elsewhere. Would this be wise? Absolutely not, at least in terms of the current state of the defense. Yet teams did call this offseason on Sweat, and while Arizona didn't make a move, that tone could change in 2027.

title: Cardinals Are ‘Loving’ Carson Beck, Insider Reveals After NFL Debut
full_text:
ARIZONA — Carson Beck fever is running rampant in the desert.
The Arizona Cardinals' third-round pick wildly impressed in his preseason debut, swirling conversations around what the team just might have in their quarterback room for both the immediate and long-term future.
Beck looked sharp in the Hall of Fame Game. Enough to usurp Jacoby Brissett on the depth chart early in the season? Not quite . The Cardinals are still high on Brissett — especially after paying him — though Beck is impressing those within the building.
From CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz :
"Everyone thinks he has a lot of potential," a source in Arizona told Zenitz. "He works hard. He played a lot of games in college and he's very mature, really smart, can process, can throw the ball and he's an alpha in his own way. It's just about being consistent day in and day out, and that's what he's been doing."
Beck arrived to a Cardinals quarterback room with two veterans ahead of him in Brissett and Gardner Minshew. Both are, at this time, ranked higher than Beck on the team's depth chart but are on expiring deals, leaving Beck as the lone passer standing ahead of 2027.
That 2027 offseason could be imperative, as Arizona may be in position to draft a potential franchise quarterback. Plenty of dominoes need to fall in order for that to happen, though the reality is Beck has to convince the Cardinals he's worth bypassing other potential opportunities.
So far, he's done that. The Cardinals saw Beck bounce back from a somewhat shaky start in training camp to make strides before his shining performance under the bright lights of Thursday night.
"He's been really sharp during (training) camp," a source told Zenitz. "He's got a shot to be a good quarterback in this league."
How the Cardinals navigate Beck's role in the quarterback room remains to be seen. Arizona won't overreact to one preseason performance and place Beck higher up in the pecking order. Beck, theoretically, could replicate those performances across all other preseason games and Brissett will still get the nod in Week 1.
That doesn't feel like it's up for debate, regardless of how Beck looks.
Yet it does increase the temperature of Brissett to perform at a high level, and right away at that.
If he doesn't, Beck could quickly emerge as a potential replacement — and that doesn't feel like a seat Brissett would get back.

title: The Cardinals Player Whose Stock Has Risen the Most in Training Camp So Far
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' 2026 training camp session is almost complete with just a handful of practices remaining at State Farm Stadium.
There have been a few players who have really stood out under head coach Mike LaFleur's watch. You have your typical stars making plays like Trey McBride, sure, though some under-the-radar names have begun to climb up the depths of the roster.
Perhaps none more impressive than seventh-round pick Jayden Williams.
Williams, an offensive tackle, had a mountain to climb in terms of making the Cardinals' roster. Late-round picks are considered a coin flip to make the roster, while more specifically a seventh-round player is often viewed as simply a flyer. If the player doesn't impress early, the team can simply rinse their hands and move forward.
Especially after an offseason where the Cardinals added multiple offensive linemen with heavy experience, Williams needed to play at a high level almost immediately to make the team. His tape at Ole Miss displayed he could perform against NFL-level players on a weekly basis, though actually doing so would be a different task.
Not only has Williams climbed the depths of the roster to make the team, he's earning high level backup opportunities. The 217th pick is earning second-team reps with the Cardinals at both left and right tackle towards the end of training camp. During rotation days where some veterans were given rest days, Williams was with the first team.
During the team's Hall of Fame Game tilt against the Carolina Panthers, Williams started at left tackle.
"I mean, there's a lot of things," Cardinals OL coach Justin Frye said a bit earlier in camp when asked how Williams has impressed.
"But I think just back to a young guy, the strain. Like we'll clean up the technique and stuff, but he's not playing as slow as some guys may early on, and just the way that we're working the rotations to try to develop the depth, find out who's the next guy, who can be the rotational guy, who could step in. The competition component to it, where you don't really know what the lights are on. Obviously, not played a game [yet], but it hasn't seemed too big for him right now, the speed of the game. Whereas he's still getting beat. But oh man ... he'll turn around and tell me what the answer is before we have to give it to him after. The growth mindset of all those young guys, and that's what he's been into.
"... I think he's just adapted really well to learning and then playing hard while he's learning, and not slowing down to try to figure it out that way."
Barring injury, we likely won't see Williams in 2026. Paris Johnson Jr. and Elijah Wilkinson anchor the two starting tackle spots while Josh Fryar is likely to be the first swing option available to fill either side.
However, Williams' quick rise from initial afterthought to capable backup just within the early months of his NFL career easily makes him a winner from training camp thus far.

title: Cardinals Respond to Injuries by Signing 2 UFL Stars
full_text:
Just hours before the Arizona Cardinals ' red and white practice, the team has reportedly signed two UFL players.
Per Zach Gershman of AZCardinals.com, the Cardinals have signed ILB Eugene Asante and TE Shawn Bowman. Both players recently featured in the UFL and fill the two roster spots left by the departures of safety Joey Blount and tight end Kenny Yeboah yesterday — both landed on injured reserve.
Asante and Bowman were two of six tryouts the Cardinals had yesterday following their return from the Hall of Fame Game . Baylor Cupp, Curtis Jacobs, Triston Newson and Bryce Pierre were the other names.
Whole slew of tryouts for the #AZCardinals on the transaction wire today. Three LB's and three TE's. pic.twitter.com/aHdvMukZYe
Asante signed with the Miami Dolphins as an undrafted free agent in 2025 after playing his college ball at North Carolina and Auburn. He then spent time on the practice squads of the Cleveland Browns and Atlanta Falcons this past season.
In January, he was selected by the Houston Gamblers in the UFL Draft. Asante tallied 34 tackles, four tackles for loss, and two forced fumbles this past season in the UFL.
Bowman played for the UFL's Orlando Storm this past season, recording seven receptions for 53 yards in ten games. He went undrafted in the 2024 NFL Draft before signing with the Jacksonville Jaguars.
Though Asante and Bowman play different positions, the goal to now make the Cardinals' roster remains the same: Excel in special teams, especially after Arizona lost their ace in Blount.
Perhaps there's an opportunity for both to earn a spot since special teams coordinator Michael Ghobrial is entering his first season with Arizona:
"One of the biggest challenges is your role in some of these preseason games is to play special teams and offense and defense. In that reveals some fatigue. I told all the guys that it is undeniable in a football game there's going to be a point where you will be tired," Ghobrial told reporters earlier this week.
"And to me that's a true test of how bad do you really want it. So when you talk about a backup, the backup could really earn a starting spot real quick. It takes mental toughness, it takes good conditioning, and it takes connection to your technique. So it's going to be a great opportunity for guys to get a lot of tape out there, and I'm excited to see these guys perform."
The Cardinals play their second preseason game on Thursday against the Las Vegas Raiders.

title: Falcons Fans Get Brutal Suspension Rumor on James Pearce Jr.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are bracing for a decision from the league office on the immediate future of James Pearce Jr., and Josh Kendall of The Athletic believes that it could be far more significant than some fans think.
The team has not heard anything from the NFL, but there is a reasonable expectation that word could come down before rosters trim down at the end of the month. Guesses from most around the organization have hovered around six games, but Kendall thinks that number could grow as high as eight, or half the regular season.
ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler seems to agree with Kendall’s sentiment, saying there is still “uncertainty” regarding the 2026 position and that how the team deals with the edge position is “worth watching” this summer. One such update came earlier Monday, with the Falcons signing Cameron Sample and moving DeAngelo Malone to the reserve/PUP list.
With Pearce’s unknown situation and the training camp injury to Jalon Walker that will cost him the season, the position remains in a worrying state. Both players saw late-season surges in 2025 that put them atop the rookie sack leaderboard, and both were expected to build on that success in 2026.
Now, the Falcons are left scrambling for answers.
The early returns from the summer appear to indicate that the Falcons do not expect to have Pearce in the early portions of the year. He rotated in with the starters on Saturday but has largely worked with the reserve units.
That could also have something to do with his absence for most of the team’s offseason program, but time will tell.
“He's doing a nice job, and I appreciate the work that he's putting into it,” Stefanski said Monday about continuing to work Pearce into the rotation. “We'll continue to roll guys in at all positions. We've had a lot of injuries now at the edge in particular. We're going to ask everybody to do a little bit more, but he's continuing to do everything we're asking him to do.”
As it has since Pearce was first arrested in February, this story will continue to evolve . In the meantime, the Falcons will continue preparing for Friday night’s preseason game with the Denver Broncos. Kickoff for that game is set for 7:00.
